content: ARTS-1, also referred to as endoplasmic reticulum aminopeptidase 1 (ERAP1), is a protein encoded by the ARTS-1 gene in humans. This protein is localized to the endoplasmic reticulum, where it plays a critical role in protein processing and transport. ERAP1 functions as an aminopeptidase, an enzyme that cleaves proteins into smaller fragments known as peptides. ERAP1 is also recognized by several other names, including ER aminopeptidase 1 (ERAAP), adipocyte-derived leucine aminopeptidase (ALAP), and puromycin-insensitive leucine aminopeptidase (PILS-AP). The name ERAP1 is the designation accepted by the Hugo Gene Nomenclature Committee. ERAP1 has two primary functions within the immune system. First, it cleaves cytokine receptors on the surface of cells. This cleavage reduces the ability of these receptors to transmit chemical signals into the cell, thereby modulating the inflammatory response. Second, ERAP1 trims peptides within the endoplasmic reticulum to prepare them for loading onto major histocompatibility complex (MHC) class I molecules. These peptides are then presented on the cell surface, where they are displayed to the immune system. If the immune system identifies these peptides as foreign, such as those derived from viruses or bacteria, it triggers the infected cell to undergo self-destruction. ARTS-1 belongs to the M1 family of zinc metallopeptidases and acts as an aminopeptidase that degrades oligopeptides by cleaving them from the amino terminus. One of its key roles is to degrade potentially toxic peptides in the cytosol. As a transmembrane protein, ARTS-1 is involved in shedding various cytokine receptors and decoy receptors, as well as trimming antigenic peptides before their binding to MHC class I molecules. This process is essential for antigen presentation to cytotoxic T lymphocytes. Clinically, aminopeptidases, including ARTS-1, are implicated in the metabolism of peptides that influence blood pressure regulation and the pathogenesis of essential hypertension. Mutations in the ARTS-1 gene have been associated with an increased risk of ankylosing spondylitis, but this association is observed only in patients who are HLA-B27 positive. The protein encoded by ARTS-1 is involved in trimming precursor peptides that bind to HLA class I molecules, facilitating their presentation on MHC class I molecules. The encoded protein can function as a monomer or as a heterodimer in conjunction with ERAP2. Additionally, ARTS-1 may play a role in blood pressure regulation by inactivating angiotensin II. Three transcript variants encoding two different isoforms of this protein have been identified.
